# Introduction

The purpose of this assignment is to explore data collection using web scraping and APIs in R.

In Section 1, I will use the IPUMS NHGIS API to access 1990 U.S. Census population data, clean the dataset, and calculate population density and water share.

In Section 2, I will use the rvest package to scrape population data from Wikipedia. I will clean the table, convert variables to appropriate data types, and handle missing values.

# Section 1: 1990 Census Data

## Part 1: Load Packages

```{r}
#| label: Load Packages

# Load required packages
# Load required packages
library(ipumsr)
library(rvest)
library(tidyverse)
library(xml2)
library(janitor)
```

## Part 2: IPUMS Authentication

I will use the IPUMS NHGIS API to access the 1990 Decennial Census data. The dataset used is 1990_STF1, and the table selected is NP1, which contains state population information.

```{r}

# Load IPUMS package
library(ipumsr)

# Set API key from environment variable
ipumsr::set_ipums_api_key(
  Sys.getenv("IPUMS_API_KEY"),
  save = FALSE
)

# Check that API key is available
nzchar(Sys.getenv("IPUMS_API_KEY"))

```

## Part 3: Extract 1990 Census Data

I will use the IPUMS NHGIS API to extract the 1990 Decennial Census data. The extract will include the NP1 table from the 1990_STF1 dataset for all U.S. states.

```{r}

# Define the NHGIS extract
nhgis_extract <- define_extract_agg(
  collection = "nhgis",
  description = "1990 State Population NP1",
  datasets = ds_spec(
    "1990_STF1",
    data_tables = "NP1",
    geog_levels = "state"
  ),
  data_format = "csv_header"
)

# View extract details
nhgis_extract
```

```{r}

# Submit the NHGIS extract
submitted_extract <- submit_extract(nhgis_extract)

# View submission information
submitted_extract
```

```{r}

# Wait for IPUMS to finish processing
downloadable_extract <- wait_for_extract(submitted_extract)

# View extract status
downloadable_extract
```

```{r}

# Download the completed NHGIS extract
nhgis_files <- download_extract(downloadable_extract)

# Check downloaded files
nhgis_files
```

```{r}

# Read the downloaded Census data
census_data <- read_nhgis(nhgis_files)

# Display the first six rows
head(census_data)
```

```{r}

# Check the structure of the dataset
str(census_data)

# View all column names
names(census_data)

# Check number of rows and columns
dim(census_data)
```

## Part 4: Data Cleaning

The original Census dataset contains 38 variables. For this assignment, I will select the 10 required variables and rename them to make the dataset easier to understand and analyze.

```{r}


# Rename and select the required Census variables
library(tidyverse)
census_clean <- census_data %>%
  rename(
    gisjoin = GISJOIN,
    year = YEAR,
    state_abbr = STUSAB,
    division = DIVISIONA,
    region = REGIONA,
    state_name = STATE,
    state_code = STATEA,
    land_area = AREALAND,
    water_area = AREAWAT,
    total_pop = ET1001
  ) %>%
  select(
    gisjoin,
    year,
    state_abbr,
    division,
    region,
    state_name,
    state_code,
    land_area,
    water_area,
    total_pop
  )

# Display the cleaned dataset
head(census_clean)

```

```{r}

# Check the number of rows and columns
dim(census_clean)

# Check variable names
names(census_clean)

# Check data types
str(census_clean)
```

## Part 5: Calculate Population Density and Water Share

In this section, we will calculate two additional variables for each state using the cleaned Census data. Population density measures the number of people per unit of land area. It is calculated by dividing the total population by the land area. Water share measures the proportion of a state's total area that is covered by water. It is calculated by dividing the water area by the combined land and water area. These calculations will help us compare population distribution and the proportion of water area across states.

```{r}

library(tidyverse)

census_clean <- census_clean %>%
  mutate(
    total_pop = as.numeric(total_pop),
    land_area = as.numeric(land_area),
    water_area = as.numeric(water_area)
  )

str(census_clean)

census_clean <- census_clean %>%
  mutate(
    population_density = total_pop / land_area,
    water_share = water_area / (land_area + water_area)
  )

head(census_clean)
```

## Part 6: Find Water Share

Water share represents the proportion of a state's total geographic area that is covered by water. It is calculated by dividing the water area by the sum of the land area and water area. This calculation allows us to compare the percentage of water coverage across different states.

```{r}

census_clean %>%
  mutate(water_share_percent = water_share * 100) %>%
  select(state_name, water_share_percent) %>%
  arrange(desc(water_share_percent))
```

# Section 2: Web Scraping U.S. Population Data

In this section, we will use web scraping techniques in R to collect population data for U.S. states and territories from Wikipedia. Using the `rvest` package, we will extract the State and territory rankings table, clean and standardize the data, correct variable types, and handle missing values. This will prepare the scraped data for further analysis.

## Part 1: Import the Wikipedia Table

```{r}

library(rvest)
# URL of the Wikipedia page
url <- "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population"

# Read the webpage
page <- read_html(url)

# Locate the State and territory rankings table
rankings_heading <- page %>%
  html_element("#State_and_territory_rankings")

population_raw <- rankings_heading %>%
  html_element(xpath = "following::table[1]") %>%
  html_table()

# Display the first six rows
head(population_raw)
```

## Part 2: Clean and Standardize the Data

After importing the Wikipedia table, the next step is to clean and standardize the data. We will use the `clean_names()` function from the `janitor` package to convert the column names into lowercase, consistent, and easy-to-use names. We will also make sure that the first row is correctly recognized as the column headers rather than being treated as data.

```{r}


# Clean and standardize column names
population_clean <- population_raw %>%
  janitor::clean_names()

# Remove the extra header row
population_clean <- population_clean %>%
  filter(state_or_territory != "State or territory")

# Display the cleaned column names
names(population_clean)

# Display the first six rows
head(population_clean)

```


## Part 3: Correct Column Classes

After cleaning and standardizing the Wikipedia table, we need to ensure that each column has the correct data type. Some numerical values may have been imported as character variables because they contain commas or percentage symbols. We will remove these formatting characters and convert the appropriate columns into numeric values. Rank columns will be converted to integers, while state and territory names will remain character variables.

```{r}


# Convert state and territory names to character
population_clean <- population_clean %>%
  mutate(
    state_or_territory = as.character(state_or_territory)
  )

# Remove commas and percentage signs from numeric columns
population_clean <- population_clean %>%
  mutate(
    across(
      -c(x, state_or_territory),
      ~ as.numeric(gsub("[,%]", "", as.character(.x)))
    )
  )

# Check the column classes
str(population_clean)

```
